opus-5.5.text:
I think they're deeply connected, almost two sides of the same problem.

If you look at what research actually is, it's not a single question with a single answer. It's a long chain: you form a hypothesis, design an experiment, write the code, debug it, run it, look at results that are often ambiguous, then decide what to try next. Any one step a model can already do reasonably well. What's hard is stringing hundreds or thousands of these steps together without drifting, without forgetting why you started, and recovering when something goes wrong halfway through. So if you want to automate research, you basically need models that can work coherently over a much longer horizon. Long-horizon capability is the bottleneck.

It also goes the other way. How do you make models better at long-horizon work? A lot of it is better environments, better evaluation, better training signals, which is itself research work. If models can take on part of that, you get a kind of flywheel: models help build the infrastructure that makes the next models more capable over longer tasks.

One thing I'd emphasize is that "long horizon" isn't just about longer context or more tokens. It's about whether the model maintains a stable goal, keeps track of state, knows what it doesn't know, and decides when to stop exploring and commit. Humans do this with notes, with intuition, with taste. A lot of research taste is really about pruning: not doing the ninety ideas that won't work. Getting models to have that kind of judgment over a long trajectory is, I think, one of the most interesting open problems right now.

So my view is that research automation is a great north star for long-horizon agents. It's verifiable enough that you can measure progress, but open-ended enough that it really stresses the things we don't yet know how to do. If we make real progress there, a lot of other long-horizon tasks in the real world will become much more tractable as well.

fable-5.1.text:
I think these two things are really the same thing viewed from different angles. If you ask what it would take for a model to automate AI research, the honest answer is that most of the bottleneck isn't intelligence in the narrow sense. The model already knows the papers, it can write the code, it can propose the hypotheses. What it can't do well yet is sustain a coherent effort over days or weeks: run an experiment, look at the result, realize the baseline was misconfigured, go back, fix it, re-run, notice a surprising pattern, decide whether that pattern is worth a detour, and keep the whole thing anchored to the original question. That's long-horizon work. So research automation is essentially a forcing function for long-horizon capability, because research is one of the few tasks where you can't fake it with short bursts of cleverness.

The other direction is also true. If you want models to do longer-horizon work in general, AI research is maybe the best training ground, because the feedback is real. You run the experiment and the number either goes up or it doesn't. You don't need humans to label whether the model "did a good job"; the environment tells you. Compare that to something like writing a long report, where the reward is fuzzy and slow. In research you get this dense, verifiable signal, which is exactly what you need to learn credit assignment over long trajectories.

What I find interesting is how the nature of the difficulty changes as the horizon gets longer. For short tasks the question is "does the model know the answer." For medium tasks it's "can the model use tools and recover from errors." For really long tasks it becomes something closer to taste and memory: what's worth remembering, what's worth abandoning, how do you not lose the thread. Those aren't things you get just from scaling the pretraining data. You get them from putting the model in an environment where losing the thread actually costs you, and letting it learn from that. That's why I think the people working on agents and the people working on research automation are increasingly going to find they're solving the same problem, whether they call it that or not.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re closely connected. AI research is a good example of long-horizon work: you have an idea, design an experiment, implement it, look at the results, and then decide what to try next. The challenge isn’t just doing each step well. It’s maintaining a coherent objective across those steps, especially when an experiment fails or the results contradict your original intuition.

So there’s a feedback loop. As models become better at longer-horizon work, they can take on more of the research process. And research gives us a setting for developing and testing those capabilities. Can the model notice that an experiment didn’t actually test its hypothesis? Can it distinguish a promising result from a bug? Can it change direction instead of spending more compute on the wrong approach?

I wouldn’t equate running autonomously for a long time with making research progress, though. A model can execute a thousand actions and accomplish very little. What matters is whether it can use feedback to make better decisions over time. That’s where research automation and longer-horizon capability really meet.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very closely connected. AI research is a good example of long-horizon work: you start with a question, formulate a hypothesis, implement something, run experiments, look at the results, and decide what to do next. The hard part is that you don’t know the right sequence of actions in advance. You have to keep updating your plan based on what you discover.

Today, a model might help you write code or interpret an experimental result, but the human is still maintaining the overall research loop. The human remembers why we’re doing this experiment, notices when we’re going in the wrong direction, and decides whether a result justifies another week of work. To automate more of research, models need to take on those responsibilities over longer periods.

But I don’t think that’s just a matter of giving the model more tokens and letting it run. It needs to verify intermediate results, recover from mistakes, and sometimes realize that the original approach isn’t worth pursuing. Otherwise, a longer trajectory just gives errors more opportunities to accumulate.

And the relationship goes both ways. Better long-horizon capabilities could enable more research automation, while trying to automate research gives us a concrete way to understand what those capabilities are missing. Can the model produce a useful finding? Can it run an experiment that actually distinguishes between two hypotheses? Those are more meaningful questions than simply asking how many hours it can stay active.

r001.rationale: It describes models taking on more of the research loop, but does not characterize research automation as expanding tool-using models into a domain beyond coding.

r002.rationale: It describes an AI research project as a sequence from question and hypothesis through implementation, experiments, and follow-up decisions, extending beyond simply writing code.
